notes.h: Why religion is a cultural indicator
notes.b: A cultural indicator is a feature that helps identify and map a cultural group. Religion is one of the strongest, because it affects how people think, live and look, and it leaves visible marks on the landscape.
points: Religion shapes beliefs, values and moral codes (the rules about right and wrong), and so it often marks group identity more strongly than nationality does.
It shows in the landscape, so a place's religion can be read from what is built there: churches, mosques, temples, synagogues, holy wells, wayside shrines and cemeteries.
It shapes diet, such as halal (permitted under Islam), kosher (permitted under Judaism) and Hindu vegetarianism, and dress, such as the headscarf, the turban and the kippah (the Jewish skullcap).
It shapes the calendar and festivals, such as Christmas, Easter, Eid, Diwali and Yom Kippur, and it also shapes names, education and law.
Census questions on religion (a census is the official count of a population) make it easy to map, because the results can be compared place by place.
notes.tip: Exams set the importance of religion as a cultural indicator as an 80-mark essay. Cover identity and daily life as one aspect, with landscape, diet, dress and festivals as your examples.

notes.b: Religion rarely stands alone. It is tied up with other indicators of culture, which is why it helps define a cultural group.
points: Religion is linked with language, because holy texts and worship use particular languages: Arabic and the Qur'an (the holy book of Islam), Latin and the Catholic Church in the past, and Hebrew and Judaism.
Religion is linked with nationality, so that faith becomes part of national identity: Catholicism with Irish or Polish identity, and Orthodoxy with Serbian identity.
Religion is also linked with politics, because religious groups often seek influence over laws and government.

notes.b: Secularisation is the decline of religion's role in public life and personal practice (a secular state or society is one not run by or tied to religion). The trend is uneven across the world.
points: Religious practice and church influence are declining in much of Europe, including Ireland and France.
Religion stays strong in many other parts of the world, such as Indonesia, so the trend is not global.
Migration brings new religions into Europe, which means Europe is becoming more religiously varied even where older churches decline.

notes.h: World religions by number of followers
notes.b: These are Pew Research Center figures for 2020, published in 2025. They describe 2020 and should not be presented as current.
points: Christians: about 2.3 billion, about 29% of the world, so this makes Christianity the largest religion.
Muslims: about 2 billion, about 26% of the world.
Religiously unaffiliated: about 1.9 billion, about 24%. The unaffiliated are people with no religion, not a religion in themselves.
Hindus: about 1.2 billion, about 15%. Buddhists: about 320 million, about 4%. Jews: about 15 million.
Islam was the fastest-growing major religion from 2010 to 2020.
notes.tip: Don't overstate these figures: they are for 2020. Remember that unaffiliated is not a religion.

notes.b: A hearth is the place where a religion began, before it spread outwards. Judaism, Christianity and Islam began in the Middle East, while Hinduism and Buddhism began in the Indian subcontinent (the region of India and its neighbours).
points: Judaism is the oldest of the three Abrahamic faiths (Judaism, Christianity and Islam), so the other two grew after it, and Jerusalem is its holiest city.
Christianity began with the life of Jesus in Roman Palestine, so its hearth is in the Middle East, for example Jerusalem.
Islam was founded by the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca, Arabia, in the early 7th century. The Hijra (the move of the early Muslims) to Medina in 622 begins the Islamic calendar.
Hinduism has no single founder; it developed gradually in the Indian subcontinent.
Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) in north-east India around the 5th century BC. Bodh Gaya is where he is said to have gained enlightenment (spiritual awakening).
Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab in the 15th century. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) at Amritsar is its holiest site.

notes.b: Religions moved out of their hearths through five main routes: empire, missionaries, trade, colonialism and migration. Each route explains why a religion is found where it is today.
points: Empire: Christianity spread through the Roman Empire, which made it the official religion in the 4th century. Islam spread with the Arab conquests from the 7th century, across the Middle East and North Africa and into Spain within about a century.
Missionaries (people sent to spread their faith): Irish monks, such as St Columba on Iona and St Columbanus in continental Europe, spread Christianity in the early medieval period.
Trade: Islam spread to Indonesia and West Africa, for example along trade routes.
Colonialism (rule over overseas territories by a foreign power): Christianity spread to the Americas, Africa and the Philippines.
Migration: Islam, Hinduism and Sikhism spread into Europe as people moved there.
notes.tip: Exams ask about the spread of world religions, with a sketch map. Name each route, give its religion and place, and include the Irish missionaries.

notes.b: Christianity split into three main branches, and each is strong in different regions. Two events, the Great Schism and the Reformation, created these divisions.
points: Roman Catholic: southern Europe, Ireland, Poland, Latin America and the Philippines.
Protestant, which began with the Reformation: northern Europe, the UK and the USA.
Orthodox, which grew from the Great Schism: eastern Europe, Russia, Greece and Serbia.
The Great Schism (the split) of 1054 divided the Catholic West (Rome) from the Orthodox East (Constantinople).
The Reformation (the break from Catholicism that created Protestantism) began in 1517 with Martin Luther in Germany, and Calvinism spread from Geneva.
Christianity is growing in sub-Saharan Africa (Africa south of the Sahara).
notes.tip: Geneva was the centre of Calvinist Protestantism. Link each branch to its regions and to the event that created the division.

notes.b: Islam is spread across a broad belt of the world, and the largest Muslim population is not in the Arab world. It has two main branches, Sunni and Shia.
points: Islam is strong in the Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and parts of West and East Africa.
Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population, which shows Islam's centre of numbers is not in the Arab world.
Sunnis are about 85–90% of Muslims. Shias are the majority in Iran and Iraq.

Mecca and Medina, in Saudi Arabia, are Islam's holiest cities, because Islam was founded in Mecca and the Hijra went to Medina. The Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca is a duty for every Muslim able to make it.
Islam is growing in Europe through migration, so it is a new religion for many European countries.

notes.h: Distribution of Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism and Sikhism
notes.b: These four religions are more concentrated than Christianity or Islam. Each is tied to a homeland, with a diaspora (a population living scattered outside its homeland) elsewhere.
points: Hinduism is found in India and Nepal and in the Indian diaspora. About four in five Indians are Hindu, and Varanasi on the Ganges is a major pilgrimage city.
Buddhism, which began in India, is now found in Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Tibet, Japan and Vietnam.
Judaism is found mainly in Israel and the USA, because most of the world's Jews live there.
Sikhism is found in Punjab, with a diaspora in the UK and Canada.

notes.b: A sketch map of the major religious regions is expected in an 80-mark answer.
points: Label the major religious regions and the holy cities: Jerusalem, Mecca, Varanasi and Amritsar.
notes.tip: Plan to include a sketch map in an 80-mark essay on world religions, with the regions and the four holy cities labelled.

notes.h: Religion in Ireland and Northern Ireland
notes.b: Census results show how the religious make-up of both parts of Ireland is changing. The Republic is becoming less Catholic, and in Northern Ireland the balance has shifted.
points: Census 2022, Republic of Ireland: about 69% Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in Census 2016.
About 14% have no religion, so the share saying no religion is rising as the Catholic share falls.
Orthodox Christians and Muslims are growing groups, through immigration.
Census 2021, Northern Ireland (religion or religion brought up in): Catholic about 46%, Protestant and other Christian about 43%.
This was the first census in which Catholics outnumbered Protestants, though Catholics were not a majority.
There is more on religious issues arising from migration into Ireland in Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.
notes.tip: Catholics became the largest group in Northern Ireland in Census 2021 but are not a majority. Use only these rounded figures.

notes.h: Types of relationship between church and state
notes.b: Countries differ in how far religion and government are joined. The four types run from religious rule to strict separation.
points: Theocracy: religious leaders rule the state, so religious authority is also political authority.
An established or state church (an official church recognised by the state): the Church of England is the established church in England.
Strict separation of church and state: France's laïcité (the French principle of secularism) and the USA's First Amendment.
States in which one church had a dominant influence without being the official church: Ireland in the 20th century and Poland.
notes.tip: Laïcité is French. The US model is separation under the First Amendment. The UK has an established church in England only.

notes.h: Theocracy and fused religion and state
notes.b: In a theocracy, or where religion and state are fused, religious law and religious leaders hold political power. Iran, Vatican City and Saudi Arabia show this in different ways.
points: Iran has been an Islamic Republic since the 1979 revolution. A Supreme Leader, a senior cleric (religious leader), has the highest authority.
Vatican City is an independent state ruled by the Pope, created by the Lateran Treaty with Italy in 1929.
Saudi Arabia's law is based on Sharia (Islamic religious law), and the public practice of other religions is not permitted.
notes.tip: One example where religion and state are fused is enough, and Iran or Saudi Arabia works. Give its date or legal basis.

notes.b: The Church of England shows an established church, and the USA and France show separation. France's version is the strictest, and it has led to laws on religious dress.
points: The Church of England is the established church. The monarch is its Supreme Governor, and 26 bishops sit in the House of Lords (the UK's second parliamentary chamber).
The First Amendment (1791) to the US Constitution bars an established religion.
France's 1905 law separated the churches and the state. Laïcité, or secularism, is a core principle of the Republic.
A 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols, including the Islamic headscarf, in state schools.
A 2010 law banned face coverings, including the burqa and niqab (veils that cover the face), in public places.
notes.tip: For France, give the three dates in order: the 1905 law, the 2004 law on symbols in state schools and the 2010 face-covering ban.

notes.b: A constitution can be secular while religion still presses on politics. India is the example of a secular state facing religious-nationalist pressure.
points: India's constitution describes it as a secular republic, so the state is not tied to any one religion.
Hindu nationalism, such as in the demand for a Hindu temple at Ayodhya (politics that treats India as a Hindu nation), has grown in Indian politics since the 1990s.

notes.b: Bunreacht na hÉireann (the Irish Constitution) reflected the Catholic majority's influence. Its religious content shows how close church and state were, yet it never made Catholicism a state religion.
points: Bunreacht na hÉireann was approved by referendum (a vote by the people) on 1 July 1937.
The preamble begins: In the Name of the Most Holy Trinity.
Article 44 originally recognised the special position of the Holy Catholic Apostolic and Roman Church as the guardian of the Faith professed by the great majority of the citizens.
Article 44 also recognised the Church of Ireland, the Presbyterian Church, the Methodist Church, the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) and the Jewish congregations.
Article 44 guarantees freedom of conscience and practice and says the State shall not endow (fund) any religion. Its special position clause did not establish a state church.
Article 41 originally banned divorce, so civil law followed Catholic teaching.
The Eighth Amendment (1983) gave the unborn a right to life equal to the mother's.
notes.tip: The special position clause was removed in 1972. Don't say it is still in the Constitution, or that it made Catholicism the state religion.

notes.h: Church influence on Irish society in the 20th century
notes.b: In the 20th century the Catholic Church shaped Irish schools, hospitals and social policy. The Mother and Child Scheme showed the limits it could set on government.
points: Most primary schools, about nine in ten, are under Catholic patronage (the Church is the school's patron, which controls its running), and the Church controlled many hospitals.
The Church influenced social policy on censorship and contraception.

The Mother and Child Scheme (1950–51), a free health-care plan for mothers and children, was dropped after opposition from the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) and doctors. The Minister for Health, Noel Browne, resigned.
Pope John Paul II visited Ireland in 1979, which shows the Church's standing in Irish life, and Pope Francis visited in 2018.
notes.tip: For the Church's influence, cover control of schools and hospitals, social policy, the Mother and Child Scheme and the 1979 papal visit.

notes.b: From 1972 onwards, referendums removed or reversed much of the Church's constitutional influence. Abuse reports in 2009 weakened its authority, and school patronage is now debated.
points: Fifth Amendment referendum, December 1972: removed the special position clause and the list of named churches (about 84% Yes).
Divorce referendum, November 1995: passed by about 50.3% to 49.7%.
Marriage equality referendum, 22 May 2015: about 62% Yes. Ireland was the first country to allow same-sex marriage by popular vote.
Referendum of 25 May 2018 repealed (cancelled) the Eighth Amendment (about 66% Yes).
Referendum of October 2018 removed the offence of blasphemy (insulting religion) from the Constitution (about 65% Yes).
The Ryan Report (May 2009) examined abuse in residential institutions run by religious orders. The Murphy Report (November 2009) examined the Dublin archdiocese's handling of abuse allegations.
Educate Together is a multi-denominational school patron, founded in 1984. Its first school, the Dalkey School Project, opened in 1978.
The debate on school patronage includes the State's aim to divest (hand over) some Catholic schools.
notes.tip: For change in Ireland, list the referendums in order (1972, 1995, 2015, 2018 abortion, 2018 blasphemy), then the Ryan and Murphy reports and school patronage. The 1995 divorce referendum passed.

notes.h: Why religion causes or feeds conflict
notes.b: Religion is seldom the only cause of conflict, but it often deepens it. Four factors recur.
points: Competing claims to holy sites and territory, for example in Jerusalem, because each side may see the same place as sacred.
Religion overlapping with national identity and political power, so that a religious divide also becomes a divide over who governs.
Discrimination against religious minorities.
Extremist interpretations of religion.
notes.tip: Keep a neutral, factual tone on all conflicts, and attribute contested numbers to their source or avoid them.

notes.h: Northern Ireland: origins of the divide
notes.b: The conflict was about national identity and political power as much as theology. Civil rights, national identity and power were central, not religion alone. The roots lie in settlement, history and partition.
points: The Plantation of Ulster began in 1609, so settlers and natives became divided by religion; it settled English and Scottish Protestants on confiscated land.
The Battle of the Boyne (1690), when William of Orange defeated James II, is commemorated by Orange Order parades on 12 July. The Orange Order was founded in 1795.

The Government of Ireland Act 1920 led to partition (the division of Ireland). Northern Ireland was established in 1921 with six counties and a Protestant/unionist (supporting union with Britain) majority.
Catholics faced discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting, including gerrymandering (drawing boundaries to favour one group), e.g. in Derry.
There is more on partition of Ireland as a boundary change in The complexity of regions (ii).
notes.tip: Don't say the Troubles were purely religious. National identity (Irish or British), civil rights and political power were central.

notes.b: The Troubles was the period of violence that followed the civil rights movement. It ran from the late 1960s to 1998.
points: The Northern Ireland civil rights movement began in 1968, campaigning against the discrimination Catholics faced.
The Troubles, from the late 1960s to 1998, killed over 3,500 people.
British troops were deployed in 1969, and internment without trial (imprisonment without a court case) was introduced in 1971.
Bloody Sunday, Derry, 30 January 1972: British paratroopers shot dead 13 civil-rights marchers. A 14th man died later.
The 1981 hunger strikes: ten republican (seeking a united Ireland) prisoners, including Bobby Sands, died.
notes.tip: Give the Troubles' death toll only as over 3,500.

notes.b: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 set up power-sharing, but Catholic and Protestant communities are still separated by peace walls, and few pupils attend integrated schools.
points: The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement, 10 April 1998, set up a power-sharing Assembly and Executive, North–South bodies and the consent principle (no change in Northern Ireland's status without the consent of its people).
The Omagh bomb, 15 August 1998, killed 29 people, showing violence continued after the Agreement. The Real IRA was responsible.
Peace walls (peace lines) separate Catholic and Protestant areas of Belfast. The first was built in 1969, and some still stand.
Lagan College, Belfast (1981), was the first planned integrated (mixed Catholic and Protestant) secondary school. Integrated schools still teach fewer than one in ten pupils.
There is more on the Agreement's institutions and Brexit in The complexity of regions (i).
notes.tip: Cover segregation too: peace walls, separate schools and integrated schools.

notes.b: Religion decided the borders of the subcontinent in 1947, and religious tension has continued in India and Kashmir since.
points: Partition of India, August 1947, created Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, which included East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.
Because the border followed religion, around 15 million people were displaced and hundreds of thousands were killed.
Kashmir is a Muslim-majority region claimed by both India and Pakistan and divided by a Line of Control. India and Pakistan have fought wars over it.
Hindu nationalists demolished the 16th-century Babri Mosque at Ayodhya on 6 December 1992. Riots followed in which about 2,000 people died.
A Hindu temple to Ram was consecrated (made sacred) on the Ayodhya site in January 2024.
Operation Blue Star, June 1984: the Indian army stormed the Golden Temple, Amritsar, to remove armed Sikh separatists.
Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by two Sikh bodyguards on 31 October 1984, followed by anti-Sikh riots in Delhi.

notes.b: Jerusalem is sacred to three religions, and the dispute over land there mixes religion with territory and national identity.
points: Jerusalem contains the Western Wall (Judaism), the Al-Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock (Islam), and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (Christianity).
The State of Israel was declared on 14 May 1948. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled in the 1948 war, an event known as the Nakba, meaning catastrophe.
In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, so these became the territory later contested.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law in the view of the UN and most states.
The Oslo Accords of 1993 brought mutual recognition between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization, and limited Palestinian self-rule.
On 7 October 2023 a Hamas-led attack from Gaza killed about 1,200 people in Israel and took about 250 hostages.
Israel's military campaign in Gaza killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and destroyed much of Gaza. A ceasefire began in October 2025.
Ireland recognised the State of Palestine on 28 May 2024, with Spain and Norway.
notes.tip: Keep it factual and balanced. Give no figure for Gaza's death toll.

notes.b: Shorter examples show religion feeding conflict in other regions. Each needs only a line or two.
points: Lebanon shares power by religious community (a confessional system): the President is a Maronite Christian, the Prime Minister a Sunni Muslim and the Speaker a Shia Muslim. Civil war from 1975 to 1990 was ended by the Taif Agreement (1989).
Nigeria has a mainly Muslim north and a mainly Christian south. Boko Haram's insurgency (armed rebellion) began in 2009, and in April 2014 it kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from Chibok.
Iraq and Syria saw Sunni–Shia violence after 2003 and in the Syrian civil war. The Islamic State group declared a caliphate (a state ruled by a religious leader) in 2014.
There is more on the Rohingya in Racial groupings, and on Bosnia in A European regional case study of identity.
notes.tip: Essays on religious conflict need Northern Ireland plus one global example.

keyTerms.definition: The decline of religious practice and church influence in society.
A state in which religious leaders hold political authority.
A church recognised by the State as its official church, such as the Church of England.
The French principle of secularism, separating the state from religion.
The place where a religion or language began before it spread.
The spread of a religion from its hearth through empire, missionaries, trade, colonialism or migration.
The largest branch of Islam, with about 85–90% of Muslims.
The branch of Islam that is the majority in Iran and Iraq.
The division of a territory into separate states, such as India and Pakistan in 1947 or Northern Ireland in 1921.
The settlement of a region by people from outside, such as the Plantation of Ulster from 1609.
Drawing electoral boundaries to favour one group, as in Derry's local voting.
A school educating Catholic and Protestant pupils together in Northern Ireland.

questions.prompt: Examine the importance of religion as a cultural indicator.
questions.model: Religion shapes identity and everyday life: it marks group identity more strongly than nationality, shows in the landscape, and shapes diet, dress, festivals and law. Its world distribution is shown by Pew Research Center figures for 2020: about 2.3 billion Christians (about 29%), about 2 billion Muslims (about 26%), about 1.9 billion religiously unaffiliated (about 24%) and about 1.2 billion Hindus (about 15%). The religions began in hearths, Jerusalem and Mecca for the Abrahamic faiths and the Indian subcontinent for Hinduism and Buddhism, and spread through empire, missionaries, trade, colonialism and migration. A sketch map of the major regions, labelled with the holy cities, shows this distribution. Church and state is the third aspect. Ireland's 1937 Constitution opened with the preamble In the Name of the Most Holy Trinity and recognised a special position for the Catholic Church in Article 44, while Article 41 banned divorce and the Church controlled most schools. Referendums in 1972, 1995, 2015 and 2018 removed these influences in stages, and the 2009 Ryan and Murphy Reports reduced Church authority. France's laïcité, set out in its 1905 law, contrasts with this, and its 2004 and 2010 laws on religious symbols and face coverings show secularism applied strongly. Religious conflict is the fourth aspect, and Northern Ireland is the main case. The Plantation of Ulster began in 1609, partition in 1920 to 1921 created a Protestant and unionist majority state, discrimination against Catholics fuelled civil rights protests from 1968, and the Troubles killed over 3,500 people until the Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998. Peace walls still separate Catholic and Protestant areas of Belfast. Religion's importance as a cultural indicator is therefore clear in identity, in distribution and diffusion, in the relation between church and state, and in conflict, though in Northern Ireland religion operated alongside national identity and political power.

questions.prompt: Religion has been a cause of conflict in many parts of the world. Discuss.
questions.model: Religion causes or feeds conflict through competing claims to holy sites and territory, through its overlap with national identity and political power, through discrimination against religious minorities and through extremist interpretations. Northern Ireland is the main case study. The Plantation of Ulster from 1609 and partition in 1920 to 1921 created a Protestant and unionist majority state, and Catholics faced discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting, including gerrymandering in Derry. After the civil rights movement began in 1968 the Troubles killed over 3,500 people; Bloody Sunday in Derry on 30 January 1972 saw 13 civil-rights marchers shot dead, and the 1981 hunger strikes killed ten republican prisoners. The conflict was about national identity and political power as much as theology, and the Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998 ended the violence through power-sharing institutions. The Indian subcontinent shows religion tied to territory and power: partition in August 1947 displaced around 15 million people and killed hundreds of thousands; Kashmir is claimed by India and Pakistan, who have fought wars over it; Hindu nationalists demolished the Babri Mosque at Ayodhya on 6 December 1992, leading to riots in which about 2,000 people died; and Operation Blue Star in June 1984, followed by the assassination of Indira Gandhi, shows Sikh separatism and the anti-Sikh riots that followed. Israel and Palestine shows competing claims to the same holy city: Jerusalem holds the Western Wall, the Al-Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre; the 1948 war and the Nakba displaced about 700,000 Palestinians; the 1967 occupation and settlements, the Oslo Accords of 1993, and the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 followed. Religion is a cause of conflict where it overlaps with territory, identity and power, so the claim is well supported, though the examples show that national and political causes are often equally important.

questions.prompt: Describe how the relationship between church and state in Ireland has changed since 1937.
questions.model: In 1937 the Constitution opened with the preamble In the Name of the Most Holy Trinity, Article 44 gave the Catholic Church a special position as guardian of the Faith professed by most citizens, and Article 41 banned divorce. The Catholic Church controlled most primary schools, about nine in ten, and many hospitals, and it influenced policy: the Mother and Child Scheme of 1950 to 1951 was dropped after Church opposition. The special position clause was removed in the Fifth Amendment referendum of December 1972, and the divorce referendum of November 1995 passed by about 50.3% to 49.7%. Marriage equality was approved in 2015 with about 62% Yes, the Eighth Amendment was repealed in 2018 with about 66% Yes, and the blasphemy offence was removed in October 2018 with about 65% Yes. The Ryan and Murphy Reports of 2009 on abuse reduced Church authority. Census 2022 shows the trend: about 69% of the Republic's people were Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in 2016, and about 14% had no religion.
